chunks: "They're points along a progression from fast and flexible to optimised and permanent, and I'd choose by the stage and the requirements.
A solderless breadboard is the fastest: no tools, instant changes, reusable parts.
But the contacts are flaky, resistance varies, and the strips add a few picofarads between rows, plus long jumpers add around a nanohenry per millimetre.
So it's good for low-frequency, low-current exploration, up to maybe a few MHz, and bad for anything fast, precise or high current.
A soldered perfboard or point-to-point wiring is permanent and more robust, and good for a one-off, but it's slow, error-prone, and not repeatable.
Dead-bug point-to-point over a ground plane is actually a classic for RF prototypes because it gives short leads.
A PCB takes days to design and a week or so to fab, but then it's repeatable, compact, has controlled impedance and return paths, and machines can assemble it.
Per-unit cost is low at volume.
An IC is the extreme: the biggest NRE, months of design and mask costs that can be huge, but at high volume the unit cost is tiny, and it gives the smallest size, lowest power and best performance.
So it only makes sense when volume or performance demands it."
